verdict.tagline: Endless stars and inventory management - explore an infinite universe with rough edges.
for_you_if: you love deep crafting and endless space exploration
you enjoy building bases and customizing ships
you want a vast sandbox to lose yourself in
not_for_you_if: you lack patience for heavy resource gathering early on
you need stable performance without frequent crashes
you dislike relying on external guides to learn core mechanics

cohorts.label: 2-20h
cohorts.summary: Players navigate an initial resource-heavy grind while dealing with technical instability and repetitive worlds.

claims.claim: The opening hours require heavy resource gathering and inventory management before the universe fully opens up.

citations.review_text:
Few games have ever pulled off a comeback quite like this one, turning into an endless sci fi sandbox you can easily lose hundreds of hours to. Repairing your starter ship on a toxic alien planet, blasting straight up through the atmosphere into open space with zero loading screens, and warping into brand new star systems still hits with pure magic every single time.

Whether you are building massive underwater bases, managing a fleet of freighters, hunting down rare exotic ships, or meeting up with buddies on the Space Anomaly, there is always another weird rabbit hole to chase. The opening hour throws a lot of resource gathering and inventory management at you before the universe truly opens up, and planetary flora or fauna can occasionally feel familiar after dozens of jumps. Still, with years of massive free updates packed into one game, it is easily one of the best space exploration adventures ever made.

No Man's Sky is one of the most incredible space exploration games ever created, and I genuinely think Hello Games deserves a standing ovation for turning what was once a controversial launch into one of the most impressive redemption stories in gaming history. 🚀🔥

This game is absolutely insane when you stop and think about what you're actually doing. You're flying through space, discovering planets nobody has ever visited, exploring alien ecosystems, building bases, collecting ships, trading resources, and somehow spending four hours organizing your inventory instead of doing the mission you originally logged on for. 💀

You start off stranded on an unfamiliar planet with a damaged ship, barely any resources, and absolutely no idea what you're doing. You think you'll repair your ship, take off, and start exploring the universe.

Fast-forward a few hours, and you're running an intergalactic mining operation, collecting strange plants, harvesting minerals, fighting hostile robots, and wondering why a random alien creature looks like somebody put a chicken, a dinosaur, and a washing machine into a blender.

AND SOMEHOW, THIS IS ONLY THE BEGINNING. 😂

The exploration is easily one of the game's biggest strengths. The universe is absolutely enormous, with countless planets to discover, strange creatures to encounter, and different environments to explore. You can land on a beautiful paradise world with lush forests and peaceful wildlife, then travel to another planet where the weather is actively trying to murder you.

Nothing quite compares to landing on a planet, stepping out of your ship, and realizing that the local atmosphere is toxic, the temperature is approximately the surface of the sun, and your life-support system is draining faster than my bank account after discovering a new spaceship.

WELCOME TO PARADISE, TRAVELER. 💀

The sense of freedom is incredible. You can spend your time doing whatever you want, whether that's exploring planets, completing missions,…

claims.claim: Planetary exploration can become repetitive, with worlds sharing comparable environments and creatures.

citations.review_text:
Few games have ever pulled off a comeback quite like this one, turning into an endless sci fi sandbox you can easily lose hundreds of hours to. Repairing your starter ship on a toxic alien planet, blasting straight up through the atmosphere into open space with zero loading screens, and warping into brand new star systems still hits with pure magic every single time.

Whether you are building massive underwater bases, managing a fleet of freighters, hunting down rare exotic ships, or meeting up with buddies on the Space Anomaly, there is always another weird rabbit hole to chase. The opening hour throws a lot of resource gathering and inventory management at you before the universe truly opens up, and planetary flora or fauna can occasionally feel familiar after dozens of jumps. Still, with years of massive free updates packed into one game, it is easily one of the best space exploration adventures ever made.

No Man's Sky is genuinely a beautiful game, and there's something incredibly peaceful about flying, across the universe, checking out alien fields, and feeling like a tiny part of something so huge, in actual application. One of my favorite things about it is the exploration, including discovering paradise planets, finding a perfect spot to build a base, watching sunsets, and simply wandering around an unfamiliar world with no particular destination in mind, in real-world scenarios.

But still, despite its beauty, the planets can, in practice, sometimes feel repetitive. In fact, many worlds are sharing comparable environments and creatures, which can, to some extent, make exploration lose some of its excitement after a while, broadly speaking.

But still, the game has a unique charm that's keeping me coming back. In fact, I love the freedom it's offering, the atmosphere, and those quiet moments when I can (to some degree) just enjoy the scenery without worrying about anything else, to a significant degree.

And yet, the feeling of being lost in a beautiful, endless universe is, by design, something truly special. Off and on, No Man's Sky may get repetitive.

single_points.text: One reviewer says base building is frustrating because you have to build on perfectly flat ground, otherwise structures end up floating in the air.

citation.review_text: The game itself is fun enough, but, I got this game because I wanted to build bases on alien worlds, while yes, you can do that, the building mechanic is genuinely the worst I've seen in any game. You have to be on perfectly flat ground, which you just won't find, ever, otherwise it'll be floating in the air. Maybe it's just a skill issue on my part or something, but I'm not spending another 11 hours just to maybe find a way to make my base not float.

single_points.text: One reviewer says the gathering system feels a bit excessive because you have to collect a huge amount of resources just to progress.

citation.review_text: The idea is very good, but the gathering system feels a bit excessive. You have to collect a huge amount of resources just to progress, and the game features too many mechanics. The concept seemed interesting, but the game itself isn't quite as compelling.

cohorts.label: 20-100h
cohorts.summary: Mid-tier players focus on storage upkeep and occasionally encounter disruptive ship building bugs.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the game as heavily focused on inventory management and storage upkeep.

citations.review_text:
This game is 80% inventory management.
Combat is monotanous; the story is a chain of fetch quests; and interacting with aliens is unspeakably dull. The bulk of the game is finding stuff and crafting, but there are far too many steps involved in crafting for it to be any fun.
And it doesn't get better.
You start without enough storage, and can't pick up all the stuff you need.
Then you get a freighter and can craft containers... and now you have 13+ screens to store stuff in, and no search function.
So, you have to create and maintain a logical system to store everything, and always store stuff in the correct screen. To say this becomes tedious is an understatement.
This game is a warehouse simulator in space.

Love this game. I can almost speak fluent Vy'Keen. Haven't gotten around to doing all the interloping I had hoped to do, though. Too busy upgrading suit inventory. Why can't I hold all these elements? And how do I find a storage container blueprint?

Absolute tons of things to do! There is a learning curve but the game does a good job to explain and assist without being overbearing. Lots of inventory management but you find out what you need to fulfill your creativity. 

Overall lots of fun getting lost in a solar system and exploring. The game performs and scales well with your system hardware. The game is more polished than some creative/crafting games. Just make sure to upload your save file before switching devices, like between PC and Steam Deck!

claims.claim: Reviewers report encountering bugs with ship building that can block access to the cockpit or result in lost equipment.

citations.review_text:
The game is full of bugs that bring a total halt to any enjoyment you're getting from the game. At it's core there's not much going on here. The variation in biomes adds as much extra works as it does maintain the freshness. The same can be said of the missions. There is enough "variety" of things to do, on the surface, but ultimately it's just the same thing in a different place. After about 5-10 hours in you'll have done everything you're going to do for the remaining 90% of your playtime moving forward. The only thing that really hooks you is the premise of building a sweet ship, possibly a fleet, and setting up some sort of operation.

This dream all comes crashing down when the interface for building your corvette is bugged, causes you to lose multi-million dollar equipment in multiple ways and overall the shipbuilding brings more problems to the game than solutions. The collision for objects in the ship is terrible, making traversing the inside of your ship a nightmare. 

Perhaps the game's complexity is stretched out across more time, but I find, at 30 hours in, I've mostly been doing the same thing I did from the start, going around a planet on foot or plane hopping, to various things to go laser. That isn't particularly satisfying. The environments aren't that varied. The problem with procedural generation is everything looks the same, even when it's completely different. The "battles" are always the same and more of a nuisance than engaging. Unfortunately, I cannot now see anything in the alternate spaceship view as it prevents anything but major celestial bodies from being rendered. Another bug with the corvette...

It's just not worth putting all that time into it just for the game to function less and less with it has intended that you make...

There are probably mods somewhere I need to install but as a base game, it's not worth it.

Nothing worse than logging on and finding that a ship you spent a ton of hours creating glitched out and now you cant access the cockpit because some random module is in the way. waste of time in my opionion

cohorts.label: 100h+
cohorts.summary: Long-term players praise the vast universe and deep customization despite vague tutorials and repetitive quests.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features a large amount of content across an infinite universe, including base building, ship customization, and exploration, though some describe certain aspects and quests as repetitive or shallow.

citations.review_text: One of my favorite games of all time! I've been playing since about a year after launch, and I've purchased this game on three different platforms over time. There is as much or as little to do as you want, the universe is literally at your fingertips in this game. There are definitely some repetitive aspects to the game, but I've never agreed with the few that call the content of the game "shallow". There are an infinite amount of things to do, missions to focus on, questlines to follow, adventures to go on, etc. You can get creative and make your own goals, or stick to the game's guidance. You can play solo, team up at the space anomaly, come across people naturally in-game (rare to do by chance), or find a community online and settle down on a system that other players flock to as well. And as soon as you think you've done it all, a new expedition or update will come out and give you something new to explore. Last time I got "bored" and took a break from the game, I came back and accidentally dumped 80 hours into it. One of the most impressive games I've ever come across, I couldn't recommend it more! Especially for the PRICE AND ENDLESS FREE DLC!

No Man's Sky is the perfect game for anyone who wants to [u]explore[/u] a galaxy. It has all the features you'd want from a game that focuses on navigating different systems, planets, and sectors. While it is a survival game, the degree of difficulty is entirely dependent on your preference. 

I've been reading so many of these "not recommended" reviews and that got me thinking... most of what they say is true! You can take on shallow quests where you do one objective and you're done. The factions and NPCs aren't wholly meaningful as you're not able to do a lot more than learn their language and do work for them. I've personally grinded earning nanites by cheesing sentinels in combat.

The fact is... no game has ever perfected every aspect of its experience. So what if No Man's Sky lacks some features or is shallow in that regard? It is a [u]survival and exploration[/u] game that can be the perfect platform for you to roleplay and [b]get lost in your own world[/b] as an astronaut, smuggler, or even a corvette designer (my favorite part of the game, really). 

If you're looking for a game where you can make your own objectives: (a) build a base, starship, or a mecha-robot, (b) find the best planet by your standards, or even (c) exterminate a hive mind of ironically mindless killer robots, this is the game for you. Besides, there's so much more content and infinitely more planets I have yet to mention. Call me the biggest Hello Games d*** rider but hey, they made a good f****** game.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the tutorial and initial explanations of game mechanics as vague, requiring external assistance or research to understand core systems and the game's purpose.

citations.review_text: This game is definitely worth a try for those who enjoy space and exploring undiscovered planets. The tutorial and explanations are vague, so I highly recommend using AI for assistance. Simply wandering around on planets won't reveal the deeper purpose of the game.

Really fun, really weird, slightly repetitive and lonely. This is not a proper multiplayer game, but you can find a lot of relaxing fun exploring by yourself.

There is a LOT of content in this game now, but NOTHING is explained to you. If you don't mind doing a bit of research, this game has a lot to offer.
